Monday. The module guide said AI tools could be used only for spelling and grammar, with a note declaring it. At midnight Aadhya stared at her half-finished analysis, and the urge to paste the whole assignment into a chatbot felt loud.
Wednesday. She didn't. She wrote the analysis herself, badly at first, and asked her labmate Ira to test her by asking why each step was there. She stumbled twice and went back to the data.
The next Monday. Aadhya submitted with a short line: "Grammar check by an AI tool." In the follow-up discussion the tutor asked her to justify one method. Aadhya answered without notes. Outside, Ira asked how it went. "I actually know it," Aadhya said, grinning.

qa.q: What did the module guide allow AI tools to be used for?
qa.a: It allowed them only for spelling and grammar, with a note declaring it.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling at midnight on Monday?
qa.a: She was tempted and under pressure, and the urge to paste the whole assignment felt loud.

qa.q: Why was writing the analysis herself the wiser choice?
qa.a: She could explain and defend it, so she really had the competence. Being caught costs less than lacking skill she claimed.

qa.q: How might the tutor have seen Aadhya's declared line and her answer?
qa.a: The tutor likely saw someone following the rule, and the question about one method tested whether she understood what she submitted.

grounding: Temptation to pass AI work off as her own where it is not allowed: she follows the rules, discloses, and understands what she submits.

"It's a closed-book certification," Gautam said, reading the rules aloud in the library. "No AI tools, no notes. You sign a declaration."

Samir stared at his practice paper. "The take-home part too?"

"Take-home too. You have to disclose any tool use."

Samir had already had the AI write two of the take-home answers. They were good. Better than his.

"Nobody would know," he said quietly.

Gautam put down the rules. "Maybe. But then you get certified as a network engineer and someone asks you to fix a real outage at 2 a.m. The chatbot won't be on the call with you."

Samir felt his neck go hot. He deleted the two answers. "I'll have to redo everything. There's a week left."

"Then we start tonight," Gautam said. "I'll quiz you on routing."

They stayed till the library closed. Samir's answers were rougher. But he understood them.

qa.q: How long was left before the certification?
What was Samir feeling when Gautam described the 2 a.m. outage?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and uneasy, his neck going hot as he realised he might not understand what he'd submitted.

qa.q: What choice did Samir make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He deleted the AI-written answers and redid them himself, following the rules and making sure he understood his work.

qa.q: How does Gautam see Samir's temptation?
qa.a: Gautam sees the real risk as lacking skills Samir would claim to have, not just getting caught, and offers to help him study.

grounding: The dialogue shows someone tempted to pass AI work off as his own where it isn't allowed, choosing to follow the rules and understand what he submits.

passage:
I'm Asif. In my final year of the law diploma, I nearly did something I'd have regretted for years.

Our course had a strict rule: essays must be our own, and any AI use must be declared. I had a moot-court essay due, a family wedding, and no time. The AI produced a clean essay in minutes. I read it and thought, this is better than anything I'd write.

My friend Manoj found me staring at the submit button. "Can you explain paragraph three?"

I couldn't. Not really.

"Then in the moot court, when the judge asks you about it, what'll you say?"

That hit hard. I asked for a two-day extension, explaining the wedding. I wrote the essay myself, using the AI only to check grammar, and declared that.

My grade was lower than the AI's essay would have got. But at the moot court I answered every question on it. I'd have been exposed in a minute otherwise.

qa.q: How long an extension did Asif ask for?
What was Asif feeling at the submit button?
qa.a: Asif felt tempted and uneasy, then shaken on realising paragraph three couldn't be explained.

qa.q: What did Asif do right, and why?
qa.a: Asif asked for an extension, wrote the essay independently, used AI only for grammar and declared it, which followed the rules and built real understanding.

qa.q: How might Manoj have seen the moment at the submit button?
qa.a: Manoj seems to have been worried for Asif and chose a question rather than a lecture to help Asif see the risk.

grounding: The reflective account shows someone tempted to pass off AI work where that isn't allowed, choosing to follow the rules, disclose use and understand what they submit.
